title: Async Patterns: Callbacks, Promises and async/await
summary: Recognise error-first callbacks, convert them to promises, see how the event loop orders work, run tasks in parallel with Promise.all and avoid the unhandled rejection that crashes a server.
introduction: Almost everything a Node program does, reading files, querying databases, calling other services, takes time, and Node never waits idly. Over the years it has offered three ways to express 'do this when that finishes': callbacks, promises and `async`/`await`. You will write the third, but you will read all three in packages and documentation. This lesson shows each style on the same task, makes the event loop visible with a four-line experiment, and covers the patterns that separate a correct server from one that hangs or crashes: parallel work, error handling and timeouts.
learningObjectives: Read error-first callbacks and convert them to promises with util.promisify
Predict the order in which synchronous code, promise callbacks and timers run
Run independent tasks in parallel and handle rejections, including forgotten awaits

blocks.text: Three styles for the same job

The oldest style is the **error-first callback**: you pass a function as the last argument, and Node calls it later with an error as the first parameter (or `null`) and the result as the second. The whole `node:fs` module still offers this form, and so do many older packages:

blocks.content:

blocks.text: Callbacks work, but each dependent step nests one level deeper and every step must repeat the `if (error)` check. **Promises** flatten that: an operation returns an object that will *settle* later, either fulfilled with a value or rejected with an error, and `async`/`await` lets you write the waiting as if it were sequential code. The `node:fs/promises` version of the same program is the one you saw in the file system lesson. For an API that only offers callbacks, `util.promisify` wraps it:

node promisified.js
blocks.content:
Node is v24.11.0
half a second later

blocks.text: `promisify` works with any function that follows the error-first convention. `node:timers/promises` is the promise-based version of `setTimeout`, which is why `await sleep(500)` reads so naturally; the old `setTimeout` takes a callback and returns a timer object, not a promise.
The event loop, in one example

Node runs your script top to bottom, then repeatedly checks a set of queues: promise callbacks (the **microtask** queue) are drained first, then timers, then I/O events, then the whole loop starts over. Four lines are enough to watch it:

blocks.title: loop.js
node loop.js
blocks.content:
1. script start
2. script end
3. promise callback
4. timer callback

items: Synchronous code always finishes first; nothing asynchronous can interrupt it. A long synchronous loop therefore delays every callback, timer and request.
Promise callbacks run as soon as the current script (or callback) finishes, before any timer, even a zero-millisecond one.
A timer's delay is a *minimum*: the callback runs on a later turn of the loop, once everything already queued has run.
`await` is a promise callback in disguise: the code after it runs on the microtask queue.

blocks.text: `await` pauses until one promise settles. Writing two awaits in a row therefore runs two operations one after the other, even when they do not depend on each other. Start both first and await them together with `Promise.all`, and the total time is the slowest one rather than the sum:

blocks.text: A rejected promise becomes an exception at the `await`, so ordinary `try`/`catch` handles it. As in the file system lesson, handle the failures you expect and rethrow the rest:

The forgotten await
blocks.text: Calling an async function without `await` (or `.catch`) means its rejection has no handler. Since Node 15 an **unhandled rejection** terminates the process with exit code 1, exactly like an uncaught exception. The symptom is a server that logs `this line still runs` and then dies: `save();` instead of `await save();` is the whole bug. Lint rules such as `no-floating-promises` catch it automatically.

blocks.text: A promise that never settles is worse than one that rejects, because nothing ever runs. Network calls therefore need a deadline. `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` creates a signal that aborts after the delay; `fetch`, `node:fs/promises`, timers and many packages accept it through the `signal` option and reject with a `TimeoutError` when it fires:

node deadline.js, when the server accepts the connection but never answers
Keep the loop free
blocks.text: Asynchronous code only helps if the synchronous parts stay short. Parsing a huge JSON string, hashing a password with a slow algorithm or looping over a million rows blocks every other request while it runs. Move such work to `node:worker_threads` or a separate process, or break it into chunks with `await` between them.

questions.question: Two database queries do not depend on each other and each takes 200 ms. Which version finishes in about 200 ms?
questions.explanation: Promise.all starts both operations before waiting, so they overlap; two awaits in sequence wait for the first to finish before starting the second, taking about 400 ms.
options: `const a = await q1(); const b = await q2();`

questions.question: In Node 24, a promise rejection that nothing handles only prints a warning and the process keeps running.
questions.explanation: Since Node 15 the default is to treat an unhandled rejection like an uncaught exception: the error is printed and the process exits with code 1.
